For structured output, \citet{slot-2025} propose schema-driven decoding that constrains LLM generation to valid extraction formats.

For NER specifically, \citet{uniner-2024} distill open NER capability from ChatGPT into smaller models, \citet{gliner-2024} introduce a bidirectional transformer for generalist NER with \citet{gliner2-2025} extending it to multi-task IE, and \citet{nuner-2024} pre-train entity recognition encoders on LLM-annotated data. These methods demonstrate strong performance on benchmarks with moderate schema sizes (typically 4--20 types). However, none systematically investigates how performance degrades as schema complexity scales---either in the number of candidate types or in inter-type semantic similarity. Our work addresses this gap with controlled experiments isolating the effects of schema size and type confusability on training-free LLM extraction.

We presented a controlled empirical study isolating the factors behind schema-induced degradation in training-free LLM information extraction. Our experiments across NER, RE, and ED reveal that degradation operates through two orthogonal channels: a count channel, where increasing the number of candidate types suppresses recall, and a confusability channel, where semantically similar types trigger intra-batch substitution errors. These channels are mechanistically distinct---the first reflects capacity limitations as types compete for attention, the second reflects semantic indistinguishability regardless of schema size.

Pairwise type confusability, quantified by the Schema Confusability Score, is a partial but robust predictor of type confusion. The signal is modest in magnitude ($r^2 \approx 1.3\text{--}1.7\%$), yet it replicates across three tasks, two embedding spaces, and survives bootstrap resampling---making it the first factor to be empirically isolated in controlled zero-shot IE experiments. Entity frequency, prompt position, and type definition quality account for the remaining variance; disentangling these factors is an open problem. We further identify a centrality confound that reverses per-type aggregation on same-domain schemas, a methodological finding relevant to any embedding-based schema analysis.

Our Schema-DAG-Guided Decomposition experiments yield an informative negative result: separating confusable types into different batches does not improve extraction, because merge amplification destroys precision across all decomposition strategies. This structural bottleneck applies broadly to decompose-then-merge pipelines.

Several limitations bound our findings. All experiments use a single model (Qwen3-32B); multi-model validation is an immediate priority. Future work should address the merge bottleneck directly---calibration-based cross-batch consistency, joint decoding over decomposed outputs, or confidence-weighted merging with better-calibrated scores---to translate confusability signals into extraction gains.

We presented a controlled empirical study isolating schema-induced degradation in training-free LLM IE into two orthogonal channels: a count channel suppressing recall as candidate types increase, and a confusability channel triggering intra-batch substitution errors between semantically similar types. Pairwise SCS is a partial but robust predictor ($r^2 \approx 1.3\text{--}1.7\%$), replicating across three tasks and two embedding spaces---the first factor empirically isolated in controlled zero-shot IE experiments. We further identify a centrality confound that reverses per-type aggregation on same-domain schemas, relevant to any embedding-based schema analysis.

Our SDGD experiments yield an informative negative result: merge amplification destroys precision across all decomposition strategies, identifying a structural bottleneck for decompose-then-merge pipelines. Future work should address this bottleneck directly---through cross-batch calibration, joint decoding, or confidence-weighted merging---to translate confusability signals into extraction gains.
